title: Management of Livestock Husbandry and Health for optimal Production and Wellbeing

lessons.title: Husbandry routines and welfare
lessons.html:
Good husbandry is the foundation

In this work experience module you take part in the daily and seasonal husbandry of the farm's livestock and help manage their health. Productive animals are animals whose welfare needs are met. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty, neglect and causing unnecessary suffering offences, and buyers increasingly check welfare on supplier farms.

The five freedoms as a checklist

  1. Freedom from hunger and thirst: enough feed and clean water every day.
  2. Freedom from discomfort: suitable shelter and a comfortable resting area.
  3. Freedom from pain, injury and disease: prevention, rapid diagnosis and treatment.
  4. Freedom to express normal behaviour: enough space and company of their own kind.
  5. Freedom from fear and distress: calm handling and conditions that avoid mental suffering.

Daily routine

  • Count animals in each camp and check water points and fences.
  • Observe behaviour: an animal standing alone, not eating, limping or with its head down needs attention.
  • Check calving, lambing or kidding camps several times a day in season.
  • Record births, deaths, treatments and movements in the stock register.

Periodic tasks

  • Identification: ear tags, tattoos or brands according to the Animal Identification Act 6 of 2002.
  • Castration, dehorning and tail docking only by trained people, at the right age and with methods and pain control advised by your vet.
  • Hoof care, shearing and crutching for sheep, and regular body condition scoring.

Low-stress handling

Use the animal's flight zone and point of balance to move animals quietly. Well-designed kraals, races and crushes reduce injury to animals and people. Never use electric prodders on the face or sensitive areas, and never beat or twist tails.

lessons.title: Health management in practice
lessons.html:
Preventing and treating disease

Herd health programme

Work with your vet to follow a programme suited to the farm and region. It usually includes:

  • Vaccinations against important local diseases, for example anthrax, botulism, lumpy skin disease or pulpy kidney, as your vet advises.
  • Strategic tick control to manage tick-borne diseases such as redwater, heartwater and gallsickness.
  • Internal parasite control based on monitoring (FAMACHA, faecal egg counts).
  • Breeding soundness examination of bulls and rams, and pregnancy diagnosis.
  • Biosecurity: quarantine new animals, control visitors, footbaths at entrances where needed.

Recognising illness

SignPossible problem
Not eating, separated from groupMany diseases, pain
Diarrhoea, dehydration in young animalsScours, worms, infection
Pale eye membranes in sheep and goatsWireworm anaemia
LamenessFoot rot, injury, footbaths needed
Bloated left side in ruminantsBloat, an emergency

Sudden deaths, blisters in the mouth or feet, or many animals sick at once must be reported to your supervisor and vet immediately. Some diseases are controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported to the state vet. Never open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly; anthrax is dangerous to people.

Giving treatments

Follow the label or vet's instructions for dose, route and withdrawal period. Restrain animals safely, use clean equipment, wear gloves and record every treatment.

Keep the vet's contact number and the state vet's office number on the office wall and in your phone, and keep a well-stocked animal first aid kit.

Record what you observed and did.

lessons.title: Measuring production and wellbeing
lessons.html:
Using records to manage the herd

Key production records

  • Birth date, dam, sire and birth weight where possible.
  • Weaning weight and date.
  • Treatments, vaccinations and dates.
  • Deaths with cause, and culling reasons.
  • Body condition scores at key times such as mating and weaning.

Calculating performance

A flock of 200 ewes was mated and 230 lambs were weaned. The weaning percentage is 230 divided by 200, times 100, which is 115%. If 12 lambs died between birth and weaning out of 242 born, the pre-weaning mortality is about 5%. Track these numbers each year and investigate when they get worse.

Welfare indicators

  • Lameness and injury rates.
  • Body condition distribution in the herd.
  • Number of animals needing treatment.
  • Behaviour during handling: calm or agitated.

Improving the system

Use your records to propose one practical improvement, such as changing the lambing camp, adjusting supplementary feeding before mating, or repairing a crush that causes injuries. Discuss it with your supervisor, implement it if approved, and record the result for your portfolio.

Safety for handlers

Never enter a crush or pen with a bull alone. Keep an escape route, wear safety boots, and do not stand behind animals in a race. Wash hands after handling sick animals or birth fluids because some diseases spread to people.

Key points

  • The five freedoms provide a practical welfare checklist.
  • Follow a herd health programme drawn up with your vet.
  • Report sudden deaths and signs of controlled diseases immediately; never open such carcasses.
  • Record births, weights, treatments and deaths to measure performance.
  • Handle animals calmly and keep yourself safe in kraals and crushes.
